source: We used MSMC2 and MSMC-IM to fit an isolation-with-migration model of the relationship between a human-specialist population from the Sahel (Ngoye, Senegal [NGO], Figure 1B) and a human-specialist population from the invasive range (Santarem, Brazil [SAN], Figure 1A; Schiffels and Wang, 2020).
evidence: This is stated as the methodological approach of the study.

claim: The analysis revealed a single strong pulse of migration between Ngoye, Senegal and Santarem, Brazil.
source: As expected, this analysis revealed a single strong pulse of migration (Figure 2A, inset), which we presume corresponds to the Atlantic Slave Trade.
evidence: This is a result of the coalescent analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: NGO has experienced substantial admixture from nearby generalist populations.
source: NGO has experienced substantial admixture from nearby generalist populations and is almost certainly not the sole origin point of invasive populations.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of the NGO population.

claim: NGO is almost certainly not the sole origin point of invasive populations.
source: NGO has experienced substantial admixture from nearby generalist populations and is almost certainly not the sole origin point of invasive populations.
evidence: This is an inference based on genetic data.

claim: Populations in Luanda, Angola are more closely related to invasive populations in the Americas.
source: For example, populations in Luanda, Angola are more closely related to invasive populations in the Americas (Kotsakiozi et al., 2018) (see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Some coalescence events between NGO and SAN may correspond to the specialist-generalist split or other historical events, in addition to the invasion dynamics.
source: For this reason, some coalescence events between NGO and SAN may correspond to the specialist-generalist split or other historical events, in addition to the invasion dynamics we are interested in.
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of the coalescent analysis.

claim: NGO provides the best available proxy for human-specialist populations in their native habitat.
source: Nevertheless, NGO provides the best available proxy for human-specialist populations in their native habitat, and the observed migration signal should largely reflect the time course of their spread to the Americas.
evidence: This is stated as a justification for using NGO in the analysis.

claim: The observed migration signal should largely reflect the time course of the spread of human-specialist populations to the Americas.
source: Nevertheless, NGO provides the best available proxy for human-specialist populations in their native habitat, and the observed migration signal should largely reflect the time course of their spread to the Americas.
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of the coalescent analysis.

claim: The study obtained publicly available data on the number of enslaved people trafficked across the Atlantic in 25-year intervals between 1500 and 1875.
source: We next obtained publicly available data on the number of enslaved people trafficked across the Atlantic in 25year intervals between 1500 and 1875 (Liu et al., 2017) and used the Bhattacharyya Coefficient to assess the degree of correspondence between this historical record and MSMC-inferred mosquito migration for given combinations of the mutation rate and generation time (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated as the methodological approach of the study.

claim: The study used the Bhattacharyya Coefficient to assess the degree of correspondence between the historical record of the Atlantic Slave Trade and MSMC-inferred mosquito migration.
source: We next obtained publicly available data on the number of enslaved people trafficked across the Atlantic in 25year intervals between 1500 and 1875 (Liu et al., 2017) and used the Bhattacharyya Coefficient to assess the degree of correspondence between this historical record and MSMC-inferred mosquito migration for given combinations of the mutation rate and generation time (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated as the methodological approach of the study.

claim: There is good overlap between the historical record of the Atlantic Slave Trade and MSMC-inferred mosquito migration across a wide range of reasonable mutation rates and generation times for Ae. aegypti.
source: The fact that we see good overlap between the two distributions (yellow-white color) across a wide range of reasonable mutation rates and generation times for Ae. aegypti is consistent with our understanding of the species' recent history and supports our approach.
evidence: This is a result of the calibration analysis.

claim: If we take the common literature value of 15 generations per year (0.067 years per generation), the de novo mutation rate that maximizes correspondence between the two datasets is 4.85 × 10–9.
source: For example, if we take the common literature value of 15 generations per year (0.067 years per generation) (Crawford et al., 2017; Gloria-Soria et al., 2016), the de novo mutation rate that maximizes correspondence between the two datasets is 4.85 × 10–9 (black dot in Figure 2A, used in Figure 2B), which is on the order of values documented in other insects.
evidence: This is a result of the calibration analysis.

claim: The calibrated mutation rate of 4.85 × 10–9 is on the order of values documented in other insects.
source: For example, if we take the common literature value of 15 generations per year (0.067 years per generation) (Crawford et al., 2017; Gloria-Soria et al., 2016), the de novo mutation rate that maximizes correspondence between the two datasets is 4.85 × 10–9 (black dot in Figure 2A, used in Figure 2B), which is on the order of values documented in other insects.
evidence: This is a comparison to known values in other species.

claim: The study used MSMC2 and MSMC-IM to characterize patterns of cross-coalescence between human specialists in Ngoye, Senegal and nearby generalists from PK10, Senegal.
source: We next sought to examine the historical relationship between human-specialist and generalist populations of Ae. aegypti within Africa using our newly calibrated scaling factor. We again used MSMC2 and MSMC-IM to characterize patterns of cross-coalescence, but this time contrasting human specialists in Ngoye, Senegal (NGO, Figure 1B) with nearby generalists from PK10, Senegal (PKT, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated as the methodological approach of the study.

claim: Human-specialist and generalist populations had similar effective population sizes ~10,000 years ago, which gradually expanded before diverging about 5000 years ago.
source: We infer that these populations had similar effective population sizes ~10,000 years ago, which gradually expanded before diverging about 5000 years ago (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a result of the coalescent analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Human-specialist and generalist populations abruptly diverged about 5000 years before the present.
source: Isolation-with-migration analysis also suggested that these populations abruptly diverged about 5000 years before the present.
evidence: This is a result of the isolation-with-migration analysis.

claim: Cumulative migration between human-specialist and generalist populations begins dropping slowly 15,000–30,000 years ago, suggesting a small amount of genetic structure in ancient times.
source: Cumulative migration begins dropping slowly 15,000–30,000 years ago, suggesting a small amount of genetic structure in ancient times, but then drops precipitously 3000–5000 years ago (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a result of the isolation-with-migration analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Cumulative migration between human-specialist and generalist populations drops precipitously 3000–5000 years ago.
source: Cumulative migration begins dropping slowly 15,000–30,000 years ago, suggesting a small amount of genetic structure in ancient times, but then drops precipitously 3000–5000 years ago (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a result of the isolation-with-migration analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The rapid divergence of human-specialist and generalist populations shows a striking correspondence to the end of the African Humid Period.
source: This rapid divergence shows a striking correspondence to the end of the African Humid Period, as evidenced by the record of leaf wax isotopes present in marine sediments from the Atlantic Ocean floor (Figure 2D; Tierney et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a result comparing the timing of divergence to climate data, supported by a citation.

claim: The study used the f3 statistic to confirm that Ae. aegypti populations in Kumasi, Ghana and Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso could be accurately modeled as mixtures of human-specialist and generalist populations.
source: Before estimating the timing of this shift, we used the f3 statistic to confirm that Ae. aegypti populations in the large cities of Kumasi, Ghana (KUM) and Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso (OGD), could be accurately modeled as mixtures of human-specialist and generalist populations (Peter, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as the methodological approach of the study.

claim: The f3 statistic tests whether allele frequencies in a focal population are consistently intermediate between frequencies in two candidate source populations.
source: This statistic tests whether allele frequencies in a focal population are consistently intermediate between frequencies in two candidate source populations.
evidence: This is stated as a definition of the f3 statistic.

claim: If allele frequencies in a focal population are consistently intermediate between frequencies in two candidate source populations, the genome-wide average f3 should be negative.
source: If so, the genome-wide average f3 should be negative, while a positive value provides evidence neither for nor against admixture.
evidence: This is stated as expected behavior of the f3 statistic.

claim: The resulting f3 values were substantially and significantly negative for both Kumasi and Ouagadougou in almost all cases.
source: The resulting f3 values were substantially and significantly negative for both cities in almost all cases (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is a result of the f3 analysis shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The use of NGO as a proxy for the human-specialist source resulted in only modestly negative values for KUM and positive values for OGD.
source: However, the use of NGO as a proxy for the human-specialist source resulted in only modestly negative values for KUM and positive values for OGD (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is a result of the f3 analysis shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The ambiguous f3 signal when using NGO as a proxy likely reflects the complex history of NGO, which is itself admixed despite its human-specialist ecology.
source: This ambiguous signal likely reflects the complex history of NGO, which is itself admixed despite its human-specialist ecology.
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of the f3 results.

claim: Non-African specialists may be a better proxy for an unadmixed human-specialist source even if the specialist ancestry present in KUM and OGD came from within Africa.
source: The non-African specialists, in contrast, are geographically isolated from generalists. They may therefore be a better proxy for an unadmixed human-specialist source even if the specialist ancestry present in KUM and OGD came from within Africa.
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of the f3 results.

claim: Denser sampling of human specialists both within and outside Africa will be necessary to come to a definitive conclusion about the true sources of admixture in Kumasi and Ouagadougou.
source: Denser sampling of human specialists both within and outside Africa will be necessary to come to a definitive conclusion about the true sources of admixture in these large cities.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation and future direction.

claim: When human-specialist migrants first come into a generalist population, their offspring will have long tracts of human-specialist ancestry in their genomes.
source: When human-specialist migrants first come into a generalist population, their offspring will have long tracts of human-specialist ancestry in their genomes (Liang and Nielsen, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ancestry tracts, supported by a citation.

claim: Over time, recombination should break ancestry tracts into smaller and smaller pieces, making tract length an inverse correlate of the amount of time that has passed since the influx of human-specialist ancestry occurred.
source: Over time, recombination should break these tracts into smaller and smaller pieces, making tract length an inverse correlate of the amount of time that has passed since the influx of human-specialist ancestry occurred (Corbett-Detig and Nielsen, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ancestry tracts, supported by a citation.

claim: The study conducted ancestry tract analysis in KUM and OGD using AncestryHMM.
source: We conducted ancestry tract analysis in KUM and OGD, as implemented in AncestryHMM (Corbett-Detig and Nielsen, 2017), using as source populations the human specialists and generalists that gave the strongest signals of admixture in our f3 tests: BKK and OHI.
evidence: This is stated as the methodological approach of the study.

claim: The study found long tracts of human-specialist ancestry in KUM and OGD, indicative of a relatively recent influx of human-specialist alleles.
source: We found long tracts of human-specialist ancestry in KUM and OGD, indicative of a relatively recent influx of human-specialist alleles (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is a result of the ancestry tract analysis shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: In both Kumasi and Ouagadougou, admixture appears to have been recent, occurring within the last 20–40 years, coinciding with rapid human population growth in both cities.
source: In both cities, admixture appears to have been recent, occurring within the last 20–40 years, coinciding with rapid human population growth in both cities (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is a result of the ancestry tract analysis shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: The distribution of human-specialist tracts was not entirely uniform; instead, they were more concentrated in a few key regions.
source: The distribution of human-specialist tracts was not entirely uniform; instead, they were more concentrated in a few key regions (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is a result of the ancestry tract analysis shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Simulations confirmed that the study had statistical power to identify mixing across the whole genome.
source: This signal could not be explained by failure to detect admixture in specific regions as simulations confirmed that we had statistical power to identify mixing across the whole genome (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result of simulation analyses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The presence of human-specialist ancestry was more spatially correlated across the genomes of individuals from Kumasi and Ouagadougou than would be expected due to random chance.
source: Moreover, the presence of human-specialist ancestry was more spatially correlated across the genomes of individuals from the two cities than would be expected due to random chance (permutation p<0.001, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result of permutation tests shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The spatial correlation of human-specialist ancestry could reflect parallel patterns of selection for human-specialist ancestry in chromosomal regions that are important for urban adaptation.
source: This signal could reflect parallel patterns of selection for human-specialist ancestry in chromosomal regions that are important for urban adaptation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the spatial correlation results.

claim: The ecology of Ae. aegypti has been in flux across human history.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that the ecology of Ae. aegypti has been in flux across human history (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a synthesis of the study's findings.

claim: Ae. aegypti populations in their native range in sub-Saharan Africa were most specialized on human hosts in the West African Sahel, where they depend on human water storage for breeding across the long dry season.
source: We previously found that Ae. aegypti populations in their native range in sub-Saharan Africa were most specialized on human hosts in the West African Sahel, where they depend on human water storage for breeding across the long dry season (Rose et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Urban populations of Ae. aegypti were more attracted to human hosts than nearby rural populations regardless of climate.
source: However, urban populations were also more attracted to human hosts than nearby rural populations regardless of climate (Rose et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The finding that human specialists emerged at the end of the African Humid Period is consistent with the hypothesis that climate provided the initial selective push toward specialization.
source: The finding that human specialists emerged at the end of the African Humid Period is consistent with the hypothesis that climate provided the initial selective push toward specialization.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the timing of divergence.

claim: It was approximately 5000 years ago that the Sahara dried and the highly seasonal Sahel biome to its south came to be.
source: It was at this time, approximately 5000 years ago, that the Sahara dried and the highly seasonal Sahel biome to its south came to be.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about climate history.

claim: Ae. aegypti mosquitoes inhabiting the Sahel area would have found themselves in a novel situation, devoid of rain-filled breeding sites for nine months of the year.
source: Ae. aegypti mosquitoes inhabiting the area would have found themselves in a novel situation, devoid of rain-filled breeding sites for nine months of the year.
evidence: This is an inference about the ecological conditions faced by mosquitoes.

claim: The novel situation in the Sahel could have driven adaptation to human-derived breeding sites, such as the clay pots used for water storage by early pearl millet farmers.
source: This could have driven adaptation to human-derived breeding sites, such as the clay pots used for water storage by early pearl millet farmers (Huysecom et al., 2004; Burgarella et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference about the selective pressures, supported by citations.

claim: Pearl millet domestication is estimated to have occurred ~5000 years ago in the western Sahel.
source: Interestingly, pearl millet domestication is also estimated to have occurred ~5000 years ago in the western Sahel (Burgarella et al., 2018), bringing multiple aspects of this mosquito's human-specialist niche together simultaneously in the region.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: There is some evidence for steady population growth and accumulation of modest genetic structure starting 15,000–30,000 years ago.
source: In addition to the signal of rapid divergence 5000 years ago, we saw some evidence for steady population growth and accumulation of modest genetic structure starting 15,000–30,000 years ago.
evidence: This is a result of the coalescent analysis.

claim: The observation of steady population growth and modest genetic structure starting 15,000–30,000 years ago is compatible with a model where some populations expanded into newly habitable parts of the present-day Sahara/Sahel at the start of the African Humid Period.
source: This observation is compatible with a model where some populations expanded into newly habitable parts of the present-day Sahara/Sahel at the start of the African Humid Period, giving rise to weak geographical structure, before rapidly diverging in response to a drying climate and the emergence of the human-specialist niche at its end.
evidence: This is an inference about the interpretation of the coalescent results.

claim: Specialist and generalist populations became largely isolated and ecologically distinct after rapid divergence.
source: Although they seem to have occasionally interbred, specialist and generalist populations then became largely isolated and ecologically distinct.
evidence: This is an inference based on the coalescent analysis.

claim: It is widely accepted that human-specialist Ae. aegypti spread to the Americas (and eventually throughout the global tropics) during the Atlantic Slave Trade.
source: It is widely accepted that human-specialist Ae. aegypti spread to the Americas (and eventually throughout the global tropics) during the Atlantic Slave Trade, ushering in a new era of vector-borne disease (Powell et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: The study relied on the historical understanding of the Atlantic Slave Trade to calibrate the coalescent scaling factor.
source: We relied on this historical understanding to calibrate our coalescent scaling factor.
evidence: This is stated as the methodological approach of the study.

claim: The results help establish the credibility of the historical understanding that human-specialist Ae. aegypti spread to the Americas during the Atlantic Slave Trade.
source: However, our results also help establish its credibility.
evidence: This is stated as a contribution of the study.

claim: The cross-coalescent signal between Ngoye, Senegal, and Santarem, Brazil closely fit a priori expectations, even without calibration.
source: The cross-coalescent signal between Ngoye, Senegal, and Santarem, Brazil closely fit a priori expectations, even without calibration.
evidence: This is a result of the coalescent analysis.

claim: Using literature values for average insect mutation rates and the best estimate of Ae. aegypti generation time would have also yielded good correspondence between the inferred timing of migration and the historical record of the Atlantic Slave Trade.
source: Using literature values for average insect mutation rates and our best estimate of Ae. aegypti generation time would have also yielded good correspondence between the inferred timing of migration and the historical record of the Atlantic Slave Trade (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a result of the calibration analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The duration and sudden drop-off in migration observed in the coalescent signal closely match expectations from the historical record.
source: The duration and sudden drop-off in migration observed in the coalescent signal also closely match expectations from the historical record (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a result of the coalescent analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Luanda, Angola was a major port during the Atlantic Slave Trade and likely served as the proximate source of many Ae. aegypti mosquitoes introduced to the Americas.
source: Luanda, Angola was a major port during the Atlantic Slave Trade and likely served as the proximate source of many Ae. aegypti mosquitoes introduced to the Americas.
evidence: This is stated as a historical fact and inference.

claim: Ae. aegypti populations in Luanda, Angola show substantial human-specialist ancestry, similar to those from Senegal.
source: Ae. aegypti populations there show substantial human-specialist ancestry, similar to those from Senegal (Powell et al., 2018; Kotsakiozi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The closest generalist relatives of human-specialist populations are found in West Africa.
source: However, the closest generalist relatives of human-specialist populations are found in West Africa (Kotsakiozi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The most parsimonious explanation is that human specialists first arose in the western Sahel and later spread to both Luanda and the Americas during the slave trade.
source: Present distributions of populations may not perfectly match their historical distributions, but the most parsimonious explanation is that human specialists (the 'proto-Ae. aegypti' described in Powell et al., 2018) first arose in the western Sahel and later spread to both Luanda and the Americas during the slave trade.
evidence: This is an inference based on genetic and historical data.

claim: The temporal resolution of the cross-coalescent inferences is relatively low.
source: First, the temporal resolution of our inferences is relatively low, and both previously published simulations (Wang et al., 2020) and our own bootstrap replicates (Figure 2B–D, gray lines) suggest relatively wide bounds for the precise timing of events.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study, supported by citations and data.

claim: It is difficult to validate the long-range statistical phasing upon which the analyses are based.
source: Second, it is difficult for us to validate the long-range statistical phasing upon which the analyses are based.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: Overall linkage disequilibrium is relatively low in Ae. aegypti, dropping off quickly over a few kilobases and reaching half its maximum value within about 50 kb.
source: Overall linkage disequilibrium is relatively low in Ae. aegypti, dropping off quickly over a few kilobases and reaching half its maximum value within about 50 kb Matthews et al., 2018; this is likely sufficient for assembling shorter, high-confidence prephase blocks into longer haplotypes in many cases.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Phase-switch errors may be common across longer distances in Ae. aegypti genomes.
source: However, phase-switch errors may be common across longer distances – potentially affecting inferences in the most recent time windows.
evidence: This is stated as a potential limitation of the study.

claim: The similar results obtained using different proxy populations for human-specialist and generalist lineages suggest that the results are robust to potential mistakes in long-range haplotype phasing.
source: Nevertheless, the similar results we obtain using different proxy populations (and thus different input haplotype structures) for human-specialist and generalist lineages (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1) suggests that our results are robust to potential mistakes in long-range haplotype phasing.
evidence: This is stated as evidence for the robustness of the results.

claim: The coalescent scaling factor was chosen to maximize the overlap between the peak of estimated Ae. aegypti migration and the peak of the Atlantic Slave Trade.
source: Another important source of uncertainty comes from our assumption that the coalescent scaling factor should maximize the overlap between the peak of estimated Ae. aegypti migration and the peak of the Atlantic Slave Trade (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated as an assumption of the study.

claim: If peak migration occurred at the beginning of the slave trade era, around 1500, the inferred mutation rate would be lower (about 2.4e-9, assuming 15 generations per year), pushing back the split of human-specialist lineages to ~10,000 years before present.
source: If we instead consider alternative scenarios where peak migration occurred at the beginning of the slave trade era, around 1500, then our inferred mutation rate would be lower (about 2.4e-9, assuming 15 generations per year), pushing back the split of human-specialist lineages to ~10,000 years before present.
evidence: This is a sensitivity analysis exploring alternative scenarios.

claim: An early-pulse model of migration seems less plausible because isolation-with-migration analyses suggest a gradual onset of migration between continents.
source: This scenario seems less plausible, in part because our isolation-with-migration analyses suggest a gradual onset of migration between continents rather than a single, early-pulse model.
evidence: This is an inference based on the coalescent analysis.

claim: An early-pulse model would make it harder to explain the timing of the bottleneck observed in invasive populations.
source: It would also make it harder to explain the timing of the bottleneck observed in invasive populations; the first signs of this bottleneck occur at the beginning of the slave trade (~500 years ago) with our current calibration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), but would be pushed to a pre-trade date in this alternative scenario.
evidence: This is an inference based on the coalescent analysis.

claim: If peak Ae. aegypti migration occurred more recently, perhaps around 1850, the inferred mutation rate would be higher (or generation time lower), and the split of human-specialist lineages would be placed at about 3000 years ago.
source: We can also consider a scenario in which peak Ae. aegypti migration occurred more recently, perhaps around 1850, corresponding to increased global shipping traffic outside the slave trade alone. In this case, our inferred mutation rate would be higher (or generation time lower), and the split of human-specialist lineages would be placed at about 3000 years ago.
evidence: This is a sensitivity analysis exploring alternative scenarios.

claim: The best match between the existing literature and the data corresponds to the main estimates of the study.
source: Overall, the best match between the existing literature and our data corresponds to our main estimates, but alternative scenarios could gain support if future research finds evidence for a different time course of invasion than is suggested by the epidemiological record.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the robustness of the main findings.

claim: This study represents one of the first applications of cross-coalescent analysis to a non-model system.
source: This study represents one of the first applications of cross-coalescent analysis to a non-model system.
evidence: This is stated as a contribution of the study.

claim: Cross-coalescent analyses are a powerful tool for understanding historical relationships between populations.
source: Cross-coalescent analyses are a powerful tool for understanding historical relationships between populations, but they are difficult to implement in practice, largely due to the logistical/computational burden of developing a large genome phasing panel and the difficulty of estimating an accurate coalescent scaling factor.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about the method.

claim: Accurate calibration of coalescent analysis is notoriously difficult even in well-understood systems like humans.
source: Accurate calibration of coalescent analysis is notoriously difficult even in well-understood systems like humans (Scally and Durbin, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: The study takes advantage of a continent-wide set of genomes, combined with read-based prephasing and population-wide statistical phasing, to develop a phasing panel that will enable future studies in Ae. aegypti with a lower barrier to entry.
source: Here, we take advantage of a continent-wide set of genomes, combined with read-based prephasing and population-wide statistical phasing, to develop a phasing panel that will enable future studies in Ae. aegypti with a lower barrier to entry.
evidence: This is stated as a contribution of the study.

claim: The same approach may work for other study organisms with similar population genomic properties; high levels of diversity are helpful for prephasing and at least moderate levels of linkage disequilibrium are important for the assembly of prephase blocks.
source: The same approach may work for other study organisms with similar population genomic properties; high levels of diversity are helpful for prephasing and at least moderate levels of linkage disequilibrium are important for the assembly of prephase blocks.
evidence: This is stated as a generalization of the methodological approach.

claim: The use of the historical record to calibrate a coalescent scaling factor may be effective in other taxa whose history is characterized by known historical events as well as events with unknown timing.
source: Likewise, our use of the historical record to calibrate a coalescent scaling factor may be effective in other taxa whose history is characterized by known historical events as well as events with unknown timing.
evidence: This is stated as a generalization of the methodological approach.

claim: Similar calibrations have been used to understand the relationship between coalescent analyses and human history.
source: Similar calibrations have been used to understand the relationship between coalescent analyses and human history (O'Fallon and Fehren-Schmitz, 2011; Schiffels and Durbin, 2014), but the approach should be especially valuable in non-model organisms where mutation rates and generation times are less well characterized.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The approach of using historical records for calibration should be especially valuable in non-model organisms where mutation rates and generation times are less well characterized.
source: Similar calibrations have been used to understand the relationship between coalescent analyses and human history (O'Fallon and Fehren-Schmitz, 2011; Schiffels and Durbin, 2014), but the approach should be especially valuable in non-model organisms where mutation rates and generation times are less well characterized.
evidence: This is stated as a contribution of the study.

claim: Human specialization first emerged within Ae. aegypti thousands of years ago.
source: Human specialization first emerged within Ae. aegypti thousands of years ago, but now, in the face of the rapid urbanization in sub-Saharan Africa, generalist populations of this species seem to be undergoing a new shift.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the study's findings.

claim: Generalist populations of Ae. aegypti seem to be undergoing a new shift in the face of rapid urbanization in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: Human specialization first emerged within Ae. aegypti thousands of years ago, but now, in the face of the rapid urbanization in sub-Saharan Africa, generalist populations of this species seem to be undergoing a new shift.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the study's findings.

claim: Positive selection during adaptive introgression can increase tract lengths and make admixture appear more recent than it actually is.
source: Positive selection during adaptive introgression can increase tract lengths and make admixture appear more recent than it actually is.
evidence: This is stated as a potential confounding factor.

claim: The study masked regions of the genome thought to underlie adaptation to human habitats before running the ancestry tract analysis.
source: For this reason, we masked regions of the genome thought to underlie adaptation to human habitats before running our analysis.
evidence: This is stated as the methodological approach of the study.

claim: If selection has acted outside the masked regions, admixture may be somewhat older than estimated.
source: If selection has acted outside these regions, however, admixture may be somewhat older than we estimate.
evidence: This is stated as a potential limitation of the study.

claim: The exact geographic origin of the human-specialist ancestry tracts found in both Kumasi and Ouagadougou remains uncertain.
source: The exact geographic origin of the human-specialist ancestry tracts found in both cities also remains uncertain.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: The human-specialist ancestry tracts in Kumasi and Ouagadougou are likely derived from nearby specialist populations.
source: They are likely derived from nearby specialist populations, with whom both KUM and OGD showed affinity in previous ADMIXTURE analyses (Rose et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on previous genetic analyses, supported by a citation.

claim: The human-specialist ancestry tracts in Kumasi and Ouagadougou could alternatively (or additionally) be derived from distant specialist populations or even invasive populations outside Africa.
source: They could alternatively (or additionally) be derived from distant specialist populations or even invasive populations outside Africa; dormant Ae. aegypti eggs are often transported inadvertently, e.g., in the used-tire trade.
